open-question.question: The runner of the VS Code extension (`gurita-vscode`) reads the project's tracked rule file to choose each task's single-task line, in its preview mode and in a looped task run. What do the preview and the run do when that file exists but cannot be read as rules, as when a line is written in no rule form or holds a pattern that Python's `re` refuses to compile?
open-question.recommendation: A file that cannot be read as rules gives no assignment, so every task takes the unresolved path the preview and the loop already carry, with the error naming each bad line and its reason. No task runs under rules other than the ones written, a person can still run the tasks in front of them by override, and no second failure path is built.
open-question.alternative: An unreadable rule file is refused whole, as above, but the refusal is carried through the unresolved-assignment path the draft already gives a rule naming a missing single-task line: the preview shows the error with each unreadable line's number and reason and lists every remaining task as unresolved, and the person may override any task there by naming a single-task line. The loop then starts, runs each task that carries an override, and stops, without running it, at the first task that carries none, a task that entered the list after the loop started included, since no rule can be evaluated for it. It adds no new behaviour beside the one already decided for a missing line name: the page, the print, and the loop's stop all follow the existing unresolved path, and a person who needs a run now can still get one by overriding the tasks in front of them. On a long list the only way past a typo without fixing the file is to override every task by hand, the pick-per-task work the rules exist to remove, and the loop still stops at any task that joins the list mid-run; the preview print must also carry a file-level error beside its per-task lines, which the preview print form, a sibling question's, has to hold.

The whole rule file is refused when any one of its lines cannot be read: the preview prints no assignment at all, only an error naming the file and every unreadable line with its line number and reason (the line in no rule form, or the message Python's `re` gave for the pattern it would not compile), and the page shows that error in place of the assignment list and offers no way to start the loop. The runner, started for a looped run with such a file, reads it before the first task and ends the run with the same error, running no line, and stops the same way before any later task at which a re-read of the file fails. Overrides made by the person do not lift the refusal. No task is ever run under rules other than the ones written, and the behaviour is one condition with one message: the person sees exactly which line is wrong and why before a token is spent, and the preview and the run refuse alike by construction. One typo in a tracked file blocks every looped run in the project until the file is fixed, even a run whose every task the person would have overridden by hand, and in a shared project the fix may mean a commit on a file another person wrote.

The unreadable lines are set aside and named, and every other rule and the default are read; each task whose assignment does not depend on an unreadable line keeps the line the readable rules give it, and each task whose assignment could have been changed by an unreadable line is shown as unresolved, as is every task a readable rule leaves unmatched when the default line itself is the unreadable one. The preview lists the unreadable lines with their numbers and reasons above the assignments, the person overrides the unresolved tasks or fixes the file, and the loop runs the settled and overridden tasks and stops at the first task still unresolved, re-judging each task the same way when the run reads the file again. A typo blocks only the tasks it could actually have touched: the rest of a long list runs under the rules as written, and no task runs under a line its broken rule might have meant otherwise. Which tasks an unreadable line could have touched depends on the rule format's precedence, a sibling question's axis: under a first-match or last-match rule it is a bounded set, while under a precedence that weighs every rule it is every task the readable rules do not settle outright, so the option is only as precise as that precedence allows and adds a dependence analysis the runner must implement and test.

Each unreadable line is skipped and the rest of the file is used as if that line were not written: the readable rules and the default assign every task, the preview prints the skipped lines with their numbers and reasons above an ordinary full assignment list, and the run prints the same warning at its start and goes on. When the default line itself is the unreadable one, a task no readable rule matches is unresolved, by the existing missing-line path. A typo never stops a run: every task gets an assignment at once, the person sees the warning in the preview where they already read every assignment, and can override any task that landed wrongly before the loop starts. A task the broken rule was written for quietly takes the default or another rule's line, the silent reassignment the draft set aside when it refused to fall back to the default for a missing line name; it is visible only to a person who reads the warning, and a task that joins the list after the loop started runs under it with no chance of override.

An unreadable rule file is handled exactly as a project holding no rule file is, both in the preview and in the run, with the preview and the run's start also naming the unreadable lines and their reasons so the person can tell the two cases apart. The runner carries one behaviour for a file it cannot use, whether absent or broken, so the preview, the print, and the loop need no second path, and the person learns one rule. Its effect is whatever the missing-file question, a sibling's axis, settles: where an absent file means refusing, this matches the whole-file refusal, and where it means a fallback assignment, a single typo silently reassigns every task in the list; a broken file is also a mistake to correct while an absent one may be a project's deliberate choice, which one behaviour cannot tell apart.

The first version gives an unreadable rule file no handling of its own: the runner reads the file as its parser happens to, so a pattern `re` refuses surfaces as Python's traceback in the preview and at the run's start and a line in no rule form is whatever the parser makes of it, and the handling is written into the follow-up documents under `ideas/` as work for a later version. It is the least to build and test for an experiment whose rule file the maintainer writes alone, and the goal already provides for leaving such parts out as recorded follow-up work. The page receives a traceback in place of the print it parses, so the preview shows a broken or empty assignment list rather than a message, and a malformed line may be silently ignored, letting a task run under a line its intended rule did not mean, the outcome the draft guards against everywhere else.
